question: A training officer wants a disciplined way to improve the wording she uses for weekly course summaries. Which sequence should she follow on each round?
options: A) Compare the new result against the previous one; name what was wrong with the result; keep the change or undo it; make one change.
B) Make one change; compare the new result against the previous one; name what was wrong with the result; keep the change or undo it.
C) Keep the change or undo it; name what was wrong with the result; compare the new result against the previous one; make one change.
D) Name what was wrong with the result; make one change; compare the new result against the previous one; keep the change or undo it.
correct_answers: D) Name what was wrong with the result; make one change; compare the new result against the previous one; keep the change or undo it.
explanations: There is nothing to compare until a change has been made, so this ordering evaluates a result that the round has not yet produced.
Changing something before naming the defect means the change is aimed at nothing in particular, and the diagnosis arrives after it has been made.
Deciding whether to keep a change before making it inverts the round entirely, and the comparison happens with nothing new to compare.

Correct. Naming the defect gives the round a target, one change isolates the cause, the comparison shows whether it moved in the right direction, and the keep-or-undo decision makes the improvement deliberate rather than accidental.
